author: AR Chemistry Institute
objectives: Students will determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Students will predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Students will distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Students will explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Students will apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Introduces the core principles of VSEPR theory and how it uses Lewis structures to predict molecular geometry.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Understand the core principle of electron domain repulsion.
Recall how to count electron domains from a Lewis structure.
Recognize that VSEPR predicts 3D shapes from 2D structures.
instructions: Pay attention to the central atom and the arrangement of electron domains.
Follow the narration to understand VSEPR's fundamental concepts.

components.text: Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other, arranging themselves to minimize repulsion.

Lewis Structure of Water:
H-O-H with two lone pairs on O
Each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair counts as ONE electron domain.

Lewis Structure of Water:
  H - O - H
      .. ..
   (2 bonding, 2 lone pairs = 4 domains)
VSEPR theory takes a flat Lewis structure as input and predicts the actual three-dimensional shape of the molecule.

modules.description: Visualizes how electron domains arrange themselves to minimize repulsion, forming the linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral geometries.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Observe the principle of minimum repulsion in action.
Identify linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral electron-domain geometries.
Associate each geometry with its characteristic bond angles.
instructions: Watch as electron domains are added and dynamically rearrange.
Observe the angles and corresponding geometry names.

modules.description: Explores the trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral geometries, and summarizes all five fundamental electron-domain shapes.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Identify trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain geometries.
Distinguish axial and equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
Summarize all five electron-domain geometries and their characteristics.
instructions: Observe the formation of higher-order electron domain geometries.
Note the bond angles in these more complex arrangements.

components.text:
Electron Domain Geometries:
2: Linear (180°)
3: Trigonal Planar (120°)
4: Tetrahedral (109.5°)
5: Trigonal Bipyramidal (90°, 120°)
6: Octahedral (90°)

modules.description: Demonstrates how lone pairs modify the molecular geometry, distinguishing it from the electron-domain geometry.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Identify trigonal pyramidal and bent molecular geometries originating from a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry.
instructions: Observe how replacing a bonding pair with a lone pair changes the visible molecular shape, while the electron-domain geometry remains the same.

modules.description: Explains why lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs and affect bond angles.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space.
Predict the effect of lone pairs on bond angles.
instructions: Compare the bond angles of methane, ammonia, and water.
Observe the visual representation of lone pair size.

components.text: Lone pairs are held by only one nucleus and occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles.

modules.description: Showcases various real molecules, applying VSEPR theory to their structures.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Observe VSEPR predictions matched against observed structures for various molecules.
Identify electron-domain and molecular geometries for a range of example molecules.
instructions: Explore the gallery of real molecules.
Listen to the narration for each example to understand its VSEPR derivation.

modules.description: Students drag electron domains around a central atom to form correct geometries.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Reinforce understanding of electron-domain geometries through interactive manipulation.
Apply VSEPR principles to arrange electron domains correctly.
instructions: Drag the electron domains (spheres) into the specified geometry around the central atom.
When you believe the geometry is correct, manually advance to the next step for feedback and the next challenge.

components.text: Drag the electron domains to form a Tetrahedral geometry (4 domains).
Arrange the 4 electron domains into a Tetrahedral geometry. Manually advance when ready for feedback.
Now, try arranging 2 electron domains into a Linear geometry. Manually advance for feedback.

modules.description: Students select the correct 3D molecular geometry for a given Lewis structure.
modules.author: AR Chemistry Institute
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR theory to predict molecular geometry from a Lewis structure.
Practice identifying different molecular shapes.
instructions: Examine the Lewis structure and select the corresponding 3D molecular geometry.
Tap on your chosen molecule to make a selection.

components.text:
Lewis Structure for SF4:
(Central S, 4 F bonds, 1 lone pair)

Correct! SF4 has 5 electron domains (4 bonding, 1 lone pair), making its electron-domain geometry trigonal bipyramidal. The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, resulting in a Seesaw molecular geometry.
